Playbook.name: Brute Force Attack Detection - IP Threshold - SOC Playbook

Reference.title: MITRE ATT and CK - T1110 Brute Force

ExecutiveSummary.Overview: The threshold rule "Brute Force Attack Detection - IP Threshold" fired on a burst of Windows failed logons (event.code 4625) attributed to a source. Triage question: is this a real password-guessing / spray attack against JCB accounts, or a benign failure storm (a service/scheduled-task running with a stale password, or a locked-out user)?
ExecutiveSummary.BusinessImpact: A successful brute force or password spray yields valid domain credentials - the foothold for lateral movement, privilege escalation and access to core banking systems. A single guessed privileged or service account can compromise the domain.

Assets.AssetType: Windows domain member servers and workstations (INTDOM), including Domain Controllers and application/service hosts

LogSources.LogSource: Windows Security event log - logs-system.security-* (event.code 4625 failed logon, 4624 successful logon)

TelemetryRequirements.Requirement: Windows Security auth events (verified live on JCB). Populated fields: host.name, winlog.event_data.TargetUserName, winlog.event_data.LogonType, winlog.event_data.SubStatus, winlog.event_data.Status, event.code, event.outcome (failure/success), event.action, event.category (authentication).

Known-population caveat (verified on JCB): Windows 4625/4624 at JCB do NOT populate a client IP - winlog.event_data.IpAddress and source.ip are null on interactive (LogonType 2) and network (LogonType 3) failures alike. The "IP" in this rule is the alert grouping key; corroborate the actual sourcing IP from network telemetry (FortiGate VPN, F5 WAF, NETSCOUT AED) when the client IP is absent.

Signal.Name: Failed-Logon Burst Above IP Threshold
Signal.Details: A volume of 4625 failures exceeding the rule threshold, grouped by the source the detection attributes them to.

Input.name: $srcip
Input.description: Source IP the alert attributes the failed-logon burst to (the IP-threshold entity). May be absent in Windows 4625 at JCB - see the telemetry caveat.

Input.name: $host
Input.description: Target Windows host receiving the failed logons (host.name). The reliably-populated pivot on JCB.

InitialAssessment.Rule: Weigh the full evidence story per the ClassificationGuidance (account spread, SubStatus reasons, and any success) - not any single fact. One account failing thousands of times with "wrong password" is usually a stale service credential; many distinct accounts failing with "no such user" is a spray.

Investigation.Goal: Determine whether the failed-logon burst is a real brute force / password spray (and whether any account was compromised), or a benign failure storm from a stale service credential or a locked-out user.

Step.name: Attempts attributable to the alerting source IP
Step.Purpose: Characterise what the alert's source IP did: how many failures, against how many distinct accounts and hosts, and by which logon types. Breadth of accounts is the spray signature.
Step.Query: FROM logs-system.security-* | WHERE event.code == "4625" AND winlog.event_data.IpAddress == "$srcip" AND @timestamp >= NOW() - 4 hours | STATS fails = COUNT(*), distinct_accounts = COUNT_DISTINCT(winlog.event_data.TargetUserName), accounts = VALUES(winlog.event_data.TargetUserName), hosts = VALUES(host.name), logon_types = VALUES(winlog.event_data.LogonType) | LIMIT 1
Step.AnalystNotes: JCB caveat (verified live): Windows 4625 at JCB does not populate a client IP, so this step is often empty even for a real attack. An empty result does NOT clear the alert - proceed to Step 2 (host-keyed) and corroborate the sourcing IP from FortiGate VPN / F5 / NETSCOUT. Many distinct_accounts from one IP = password spray; one account with high fails = targeted guessing or a stale credential.

Step.name: Failed-logon burst on the targeted host
Step.Purpose: The reliably-populated JCB view: how the failures distribute across accounts on the targeted host, and the SubStatus reasons that separate a spray from a service-account misconfiguration.
Step.Query: FROM logs-system.security-* | WHERE event.code == "4625" AND host.name == "$host" AND @timestamp >= NOW() - 4 hours | STATS fails = COUNT(*), distinct_accounts = COUNT_DISTINCT(winlog.event_data.TargetUserName), accounts = VALUES(winlog.event_data.TargetUserName), logon_types = VALUES(winlog.event_data.LogonType), sub_status = VALUES(winlog.event_data.SubStatus) | LIMIT 1
Step.AnalystNotes: SubStatus decode: 0xc0000064 = user name does not exist (username enumeration / spray hallmark); 0xc000006a = wrong password (targeted guessing OR a stale service/app credential); 0xc0000072 = account disabled; 0xc0000234 = account locked out; 0xc0000071 = password expired. Many distinct_accounts + 0xc0000064 = spray (escalate). One account + thousands of 0xc000006a on the same app/service host = almost always a stale service credential (misconfiguration).

Step.name: Successful logon after failures (breach check)
Step.Purpose: The decisive signal: an account that logged on successfully (4624) on the same host during the failure burst may indicate a guessed password. Compare per-account success vs failure counts.
Step.Query: FROM logs-system.security-* | WHERE event.code IN ("4624","4625") AND host.name == "$host" AND @timestamp >= NOW() - 4 hours | STATS attempts = COUNT(*) BY event.code, winlog.event_data.TargetUserName | SORT attempts DESC | LIMIT 20
Step.AnalystNotes: An account showing both many 4625 failures AND a 4624 success in the same window is the highest-priority finding - treat as a possible successful brute force and pivot to that account's post-logon activity. Pure failures with no matching success supports spray-without-success (still credential-access, but no confirmed compromise).

Node.Condition: An account shows many 4625 failures AND a 4624 success on the same host in the window (INV-03), or many distinct accounts are targeted from one source with 0xc0000064 (INV-01/INV-02).
Node.Result: True Positive (Brute Force / Password Spray - possible credential compromise)

Node.Condition: A single account fails thousands of times with 0xc000006a (wrong password) on an application/service host, matching a known service or scheduled task with a stale credential.
Node.Result: Misconfiguration (stale service/app credential - not an attack)

Node.Condition: Failures resolve to a known locked-out or recently-password-changed user re-trying from their own workstation, with no account breadth and no success.
Node.Result: False Positive (authorised user / benign failure storm)

Node.Condition: Real account breadth or an external-sourced burst, but the sourcing IP and scope cannot be established from available telemetry.
Node.Result: Needs Escalation (corroborate source via FortiGate VPN / F5 / NETSCOUT; hand to SOC L2)

FalsePositive.Definition: An authorised or proven-benign failure storm: a stale service/scheduled-task credential, or a locked-out / recently-changed user re-trying - not an adversary guessing passwords.

Indicators.Item: One (or very few) accounts, high failure count, SubStatus dominated by 0xc000006a (wrong password).
Target account is a service/app account (e.g. svc_*, *_srv) and the host is its application server.
No 4624 success for the failing account; no account breadth (spray).

SOCAction.Item: Confirm the account/host is a known service or a locked-out user; document the owning system; close as benign/misconfiguration and refer the stale credential to the system owner for rotation.

TruePositive.Definition: An adversary guessing credentials: many distinct accounts from one source (spray), sustained targeted guessing of one account, or any failure burst followed by a success.

Indicators.Item: Many distinct target accounts in a short window (spray), especially with 0xc0000064 (unknown user - enumeration).
A 4624 success for an account that also has a wall of 4625 failures (possible guessed password).
Targeting of privileged or service accounts, or a burst sourced from outside normal working hours / an unexpected host.

SOCAction.Item: If a success is present: treat the account as compromised - force password reset, revoke sessions, and investigate post-logon activity. Otherwise: reset/tighten targeted accounts, block/monitor the corroborated source, and hunt for the same source across VPN/WAF telemetry.

Phase.name: Immediate Actions (0-30 minutes)
Phase.Action: Determine from INV-03 whether any targeted account also succeeded (4624). If yes, treat that account as compromised immediately.
Establish the scope from INV-02: single account (likely service/misconfig) vs many accounts (spray). Capture the target host and account list.
If the client IP is absent, corroborate the source from FortiGate VPN / F5 / NETSCOUT telemetry for the same window before concluding.

Phase.name: Containment and Eradication (hours)
Phase.Action: For confirmed compromise: force password reset and revoke active sessions/Kerberos tickets for the account; block the corroborated source IP at the perimeter; review the account's logons and actions after the success.
For a spray without success: reset any weak/targeted accounts, enforce lockout/MFA where missing, and blocklist the source.

Phase.name: Recovery and Hardening (days)
Phase.Action: Rotate stale service/scheduled-task credentials that generate benign failure storms so they stop masking real attacks; review account-lockout and MFA policy; add the source and pattern to hunting.

Escalation.Trigger: A 4624 success amid the failure burst (possible compromise), targeting of privileged/service accounts, or an external brute force whose source must be corroborated across VPN/WAF telemetry.

FalsePositiveClosure.Item: Benign storm confirmed (stale service credential or locked-out user); owning system and remediation (credential rotation) documented; no account breadth and no success.

TruePositiveClosure.Item: Compromised or targeted accounts reset and sessions revoked; source corroborated and blocked; post-compromise activity reviewed; spray/guessing pattern documented and added to hunting.
